title: Ictal visual hallucinations due to frontal lobe epilepsy in a patient with bipolar disorder☆
case_prompt:
A 75-year-old man with a 10-year history of bipolar disorder managed on duloxetine, quetiapine, and lorazepam and started on sodium valproate one month earlier presented to the emergency department after a transient episode of confusion. He had transient inability to speak, an open mouth with simple vocalizations, and reached toward his wife’s face as if to cover it. The episode lasted a few minutes, after which he described a foreign-body sensation in his throat accompanied by agitation, fear, and disgust. He was treated with intravenous lorazepam for a presumed panic attack and discharged.

A few hours later, a similar event occurred, and he was admitted. He had stopped sodium valproate four days earlier. On admission he was alert, oriented, and communicative; neurologic examination was normal; routine blood tests, including liver function, thyroid studies, and viral and syphilis serologies, were unremarkable. During the first hospital day, he had 5–7 stereotyped episodes in which he moved his hands as if extracting something from his mouth and simultaneously covered bystanders’ eyes. He remained awake but unresponsive to verbal questions, with episodes lasting minutes and followed by brief confusion with anxiety and stuttering that resolved completely afterward. He then reported that, during each event, he saw a multicolored, snake-like animal emerging from his throat, preventing him from speaking, and felt intense disgust and fear while trying to hide the vision by covering others’ eyes. A psychiatric consultation diagnosed a psychotic disorder complicating depression and recommended increasing quetiapine to 150 mg/day.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Panic attack suspected — “an anxiety disorder such as a panic attack was suspected…”  
2. Psychotic disorder secondary to depression — “A psychiatric evaluation diagnosed the psychotic disorder as a complication of depression and suggested an increase in the dosage of quetiapine…”  
3. Infective encephalitis ruled out — “Cerebrospinal fluid investigations excluded infective encephalitis.”  
4. Primary psychiatric psychosis considered but atypical — “epileptic hallucinatory states are often indistinguishable from those in the primary psychosis, although these almost always have additional epileptic features such as confusion or altered awareness.”  
5. Frontal epileptic seizure confirmed by EEG — “Ictal EEG showed the sudden appearance of continuous rhythmic spikes at a frequency of 5 Hz/s localized on the frontal regions bilaterally and lasting 40 s…”
